description: An exploration of salts: their nature, types, methods of preparation for soluble and insoluble salts, solubility rules, water of crystallisation, and everyday uses.

mcq.questionText: A salt is best described as a compound formed when the hydrogen ion of an acid is replaced by which of the following?

options.text: A metal ion or the ammonium ion

mcq.explanation: A salt is produced when the replaceable hydrogen ion(s) of an acid are replaced by a metal ion or the ammonium ion (NH4+).

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an example of a normal salt?
mcq.explanation: A normal salt has all the replaceable hydrogen ions of the acid completely replaced by a metal; NaCl is a normal salt.

mcq.questionText: An acid salt is formed when:

options.text: All the replaceable hydrogen ions of the acid are replaced
Only some of the replaceable hydrogen ions of the acid are replaced
A metal oxide reacts with water

mcq.explanation: An acid salt still contains replaceable hydrogen because only part of the acid's hydrogen ions have been replaced by a metal, e.g. NaHSO4.

mcq.questionText: Which method is most suitable for preparing an insoluble salt such as barium sulphate?

options.text: Action of acid on a metal

mcq.explanation: Insoluble salts are made by mixing two soluble solutions so that the insoluble salt precipitates out and can be filtered off.

mcq.questionText: Which one of the following salts is generally INSOLUBLE in water?
mcq.explanation: Most chlorides are soluble, but silver chloride (and lead chloride) are exceptions that are insoluble in water.

mcq.questionText: When dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with zinc metal, the products are:
mcq.explanation: An acid reacting with a reactive metal produces a salt and hydrogen gas: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

mcq.questionText: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, which gas is always released?
mcq.explanation: Acid plus carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

mcq.questionText: The reaction between an acid and a base or alkali to form a salt and water only is called:
mcq.explanation: Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base/alkali to give a salt and water.

options.text: Water added when dissolving a salt
A fixed number of water molecules chemically combined in the crystal structure of a salt
Water used to wash a precipitate

mcq.explanation: Water of crystallisation is the definite proportion of water molecules chemically combined within the crystals of a hydrated salt.

mcq.questionText: The blue colour of hydrated copper(II) sulphate crystals (CuSO4.5H2O) is due to:
mcq.explanation: The blue colour is caused by the water of crystallisation; on heating, the anhydrous salt turns white.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following salts can be prepared by the action of an acid on a metal?

options.text: Sodium chloride (using sodium metal in acid)
Silver nitrate (using silver metal in dilute acid)

mcq.explanation: Magnesium is reactive but safe enough to react steadily with dilute sulphuric acid to give magnesium sulphate and hydrogen; copper and silver are too unreactive, and sodium is dangerously reactive.

mcq.questionText: Which group of salts is ALWAYS soluble in water regardless of the metal present?
mcq.explanation: All nitrates are soluble in water. Most carbonates, sulphides and phosphates are insoluble.

mcq.questionText: In preparing a soluble salt by neutralisation of an alkali with an acid, an indicator is used because:

options.text: It shows the exact point when the acid has just neutralised the alkali
It makes the salt crystals larger

mcq.explanation: An indicator marks the end point so the correct volumes are noted; the experiment is then repeated without indicator to get a pure salt.

mcq.questionText: A salt commonly used as table salt and to preserve food is:
mcq.explanation: Sodium chloride (common salt) is used to season and preserve food.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a basic salt?
mcq.explanation: A basic salt contains hydroxide or oxide ions in addition to the normal salt anion; basic copper carbonate is an example.

fib.questionText: A compound formed when the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion is called a _____.
fib.explanation: This is the basic definition of a salt.

fib.questionText: A salt in which all the replaceable hydrogen ions of the acid have been completely replaced by a metal is called a _____ salt.
fib.explanation: Normal salts contain no replaceable hydrogen, e.g. NaCl, Na2SO4.

fib.questionText: The method used to prepare an insoluble salt by mixing two solutions is called _____.
fib.explanation: Precipitation (double decomposition) forms an insoluble salt that is then filtered off.

fib.questionText: When dilute sulphuric acid reacts with magnesium, the salt formed is magnesium _____.
fib.explanation: Sulphuric acid produces sulphate salts: Mg + H2SO4 -> MgSO4 + H2.

fib.questionText: The water molecules chemically combined in a fixed proportion within crystals of a salt are called water of _____.
fib.explanation: Hydrated salts contain water of crystallisation, e.g. CuSO4.5H2O.

fib.questionText: A salt that contains no water of crystallisation is described as _____.
fib.explanation: Anhydrous salts have lost their water of crystallisation, e.g. white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate.

fib.questionText: All sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are _____ in water.
fib.explanation: These salts are always soluble, a key part of the solubility rules.

fib.questionText: When an acid reacts with a carbonate, the three products formed are a salt, water and _____ gas.
fib.explanation: Acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide.

fib.questionText: The process of forming pure salt crystals from a saturated salt solution by slow cooling or evaporation is called _____.
fib.explanation: Crystallisation is used to obtain pure crystals of a soluble salt.

fib.questionText: A salt that still contains replaceable hydrogen ions from the acid is called an _____ salt.
fib.explanation: Acid salts, such as NaHCO3 and NaHSO4, have only partial replacement of the acid's hydrogen.

tf.questionText: A salt is formed when a metal ion replaces the hydrogen ion of an acid.
tf.explanation: This describes how salts are formed from acids.

tf.questionText: All salts are soluble in water.
tf.explanation: Many salts such as silver chloride and barium sulphate are insoluble in water.

tf.questionText: Insoluble salts are usually prepared by the precipitation method.
tf.explanation: Mixing two soluble solutions produces an insoluble salt that is filtered off.

tf.questionText: Sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3) is an example of a normal salt.
tf.explanation: It is an acid salt because it still contains a replaceable hydrogen ion.

tf.questionText: When a hydrated salt is heated strongly, it loses its water of crystallisation.
tf.explanation: Heating drives off the water of crystallisation, leaving the anhydrous salt.

tf.questionText: All nitrate salts are insoluble in water.
tf.explanation: All nitrates are in fact soluble in water.

tf.questionText: Copper metal reacts vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid to give a salt and hydrogen.
tf.explanation: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid.

tf.questionText: Neutralisation of an acid with an alkali produces a salt and water only.
tf.explanation: Acid + alkali -> salt + water is the neutralisation reaction.

tf.questionText: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is blue in colour.
tf.explanation: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate is white; it turns blue when water is added.

tf.questionText: A soluble salt can be obtained from its solution by the process of crystallisation.
tf.explanation: Evaporating to saturation and cooling allows pure crystals of a soluble salt to form.

summary.correctAnswer: A compound formed when the hydrogen ion of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
summary.explanation: Salts are derived from acids by replacing replaceable hydrogen.

summary.correctAnswer: Normal salts, acid salts and basic salts.
summary.explanation: They differ in whether hydrogen is fully replaced, partly replaced, or hydroxide/oxide is present.

summary.correctAnswer: A salt with all replaceable hydrogen of the acid replaced by a metal, e.g. NaCl.
A salt that still contains replaceable hydrogen, e.g. NaHCO3, NaHSO4.
summary.explanation: Formed by partial replacement of the acid's hydrogen.

summary.correctAnswer: Acid on a metal, acid on a base/oxide, acid on a carbonate, and neutralisation of an acid with an alkali.
summary.explanation: Soluble salts are recovered by evaporation and crystallisation.

summary.correctAnswer: Precipitation: mixing two soluble solutions, then filtering, washing and drying the precipitate.

summary.questionText: Solubility rule for nitrates and group I/ammonium salts
summary.correctAnswer: All nitrates and all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts are soluble in water.
summary.explanation: These are reliable soluble groups in the solubility rules.

summary.correctAnswer: Silver chloride, lead chloride, barium sulphate and most carbonates are insoluble.
summary.explanation: Used in precipitation reactions and tests.

summary.correctAnswer: A fixed number of water molecules chemically combined in the crystals of a hydrated salt.
summary.explanation: Lost on heating to give the anhydrous salt.

summary.correctAnswer: Sodium chloride for food, fertilisers (ammonium salts), medicine, and copper sulphate as a fungicide.
summary.explanation: Salts have many domestic, agricultural and industrial uses.

hoq.questionText: A student wants to prepare pure crystals of soluble copper(II) sulphate. Which of the following sets of steps is most appropriate?

options.text: Mix copper(II) sulphate solution with sodium hydroxide and filter the precipitate
Add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulphuric acid, filter off the excess, then evaporate and crystallise the filtrate
Add copper metal to dilute hydrochloric acid and evaporate
Mix sodium sulphate solution with copper nitrate solution and dry

hoq.explanation: Excess insoluble copper(II) oxide ensures all acid reacts; the unreacted oxide is filtered off and the salt is recovered by crystallisation.

hoq.questionText: 5.0 g of a hydrated salt was heated until its mass became constant at 3.2 g. What conclusion can be drawn?

options.text: The salt gained 1.8 g of oxygen during heating
The salt lost 1.8 g of water of crystallisation
The salt decomposed completely into gases

hoq.explanation: The loss in mass (5.0 - 3.2 = 1.8 g) is the water of crystallisation driven off, leaving the anhydrous salt.

hoq.questionText: Why can an insoluble salt like lead(II) iodide NOT be prepared by adding dilute acid to lead metal, but barium sulphate can be made by precipitation?

options.text: Because lead is more reactive than barium
Because insoluble salts cannot be separated by evaporation, so they are best made by mixing two solutions that form a precipitate
Because acids never react with metals
Because barium sulphate is soluble in water

hoq.explanation: Insoluble salts are obtained by precipitation and filtration, not by evaporating a solution, since they will not stay dissolved.
